Thanks for the suggestion. uv doesn't have a `uv shell` command, but the docs cover the two ways to work in a project environment.

To use `uv run` (no activation needed), prefix your command with it, e.g. `uv run python -c "import example"` or `uv run pytest`. `uv run` syncs the environment first, so it's up to date.

To activate the environment manually, run `uv sync` and then activate it:

- macOS/Linux: `source .venv/bin/activate` (`activate.fish`, `activate.csh`, and `activate.nu` are also provided for those shells)
- Windows: `.venv\Scripts\activate`

If `.venv` is missing, `uv sync` (or any `uv run`) will create it.

reply: Thanks for the suggestion. uv doesn't replace its own process with the command it runs (no `execv`). It runs the command as a child process so it can report better errors on failure. On Unix, uv forwards most signals to the child; a SIGINT is forwarded only if it's sent more than once or the child's process group differs from uv's. On Windows, uv ignores Ctrl-C and leaves handling to the child. See the "Signal handling" section of the `uv run` docs for details.

Thanks for the report! uv has no dedicated rename syntax, but scoped overrides combined with scoped exclusions cover this case. For FuelSDK, you can swap `suds-jurko` for `suds` only for FuelSDK's requirements:

```toml
[tool.uv]
override-dependencies = [
    { package = { name = "fuelsdk" }, dependencies = ["suds"] },
]
exclude-dependencies = [
    { package = { name = "fuelsdk" }, dependencies = ["suds-jurko"] },
]
```

Then add `suds` to your project's dependencies. The `version` field can be added to `package` to target a specific FuelSDK release. Use `exclude-dependencies = ["suds-jurko"]` (without a scope) to remove a dependency everywhere. The docs don't cover a standalone rename syntax for overrides files, so that part of your request is a feature suggestion for a maintainer to consider.

Thanks for the report. This follows from uv's default behavior. PySide6 6.8.1.1 has no source distribution, and by default uv only requires such a package to have a wheel for the target Python version, not for every platform. The lockfile can therefore include 6.8.1.1 even though it has no Windows wheel.

To have uv backtrack to a release that covers Windows, declare the platforms you support in `required-environments`:

```toml
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
    "sys_platform == 'win32' and platform_machine == 'AMD64'",
]
```

With this set, uv skips releases that lack a compatible wheel for that environment, so it should select 6.8.1 on Windows. Add your other platforms (for example macOS or Linux) to the same list so the lockfile covers them too.

Thanks for the report. This is tracked in uv#4422, which asks for the same thing: removing a dependency entirely, not just changing its version range.

uv now has a dedicated way to do this. Add the package to `exclude-dependencies` in `[tool.uv]`:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-dependencies = ["typing-extensions"]
```

To drop it only for one parent package, use the scoped form:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-dependencies = [
    { package = { name = "bar", version = "0.0.5" }, dependencies = ["typing-extensions"] },
]
```

If you're on an older uv without this, the workaround from #4422 is an override with a never-true marker, e.g. `"typing-extensions ; sys_platform == 'never'"`.

Thanks for the report. This is a duplicate of #10008, which covers the same gap: `uv export` can't write index configuration to `requirements.txt`.

The `--index`, `--extra-index-url`, and `--index-url` flags apply to commands that resolve, but the `requirements.txt` format has no way to express index pinning or uv's index strategies, so the export omits them. Packages pinned to a non-default index, such as the `torch` example in #10008, can end up with output that won't install as written.

As suggested in #10008, the workaround is to export to `pylock.toml` (PEP 751), which doesn't have this limitation:

```console
$ uv export --format pylock.toml -o pylock.toml
```

Please follow #10008 for updates.

Thanks for the report. uv's docs cover pointing a dependency at a local wheel with a path source. In `pyproject.toml`, add a `tool.uv.sources` entry for `opencv-python` that points to your custom `.whl`:

```toml
[tool.uv.sources]
opencv-python = { path = "wheels/my_opencv-<version>-cp312-cp312-linux_x86_64.whl" }
```

Then run `uv lock` and `uv sync`, so the locked environment uses your wheel instead of PyPI's `opencv-python`. Path sources are documented under "Dependency sources > Path" in the dependencies guide.

This only applies to a uv-managed project. Installing a wheel with `uv pip install` before `uv pip install -r pyproject.toml` won't reliably replace the dependency, because the second command resolves `opencv-python` again.

Also check that the wheel's METADATA and import name match what the library expects. The `recursion is detected during loading of "cv2"` error comes from OpenCV's own packaging, not from uv.

This is a duplicate of #2500. The root cause is the same: `uv pip` only inspects the interpreter's own `purelib`/`platlib` site-packages and doesn't look at the other `sys.path` entries, so packages in the system site-packages (here, `tree-sitter-markdown` installed by Termux's `pkg`) aren't seen. uv then tries to build the package from source, which fails on Termux.

Tracking progress on the fix is in #2500. Until then, you can install the package into the venv with `uv pip install --no-deps` only if you're fine with a copy in the venv, or use a venv without `--system-site-packages` and install the Termux package's dependencies directly.
